title: Bildad Again: The Lamp of the Wicked Goes Out
summary: Bildad speaks a second time, offended that Job treats the friends as stupid. He describes the fate of the wicked in a series of grim images: his lamp goes out, his own feet lead him into traps, terrors chase him, disease eats his skin, and he is marched off to the king of terrors. His tent burns, his roots dry up, his name is forgotten, and he leaves no children behind.
story: The second round of speeches is under way. Eliphaz has described the wicked man's ruin (chapter 15), and Job has answered with his most violent description of God's attack and his boldest hope of a witness in heaven (chapters 16 and 17). Bildad does not respond to that hope at all. Instead he gives the most concentrated portrait of the wicked man's end in the book, and like Eliphaz he offers Job no path back. In chapter 8 Bildad at least promised that God would fill Job's mouth with laughter if he were pure. Here the promise is gone. Job's reply in chapter 19 will be one of the book's great turning points, and it grows directly out of the despair Bildad's words intensify.
historical:
Several images in Bildad's speech draw on the religious language of Israel's neighbors. The king of terrors (verse 14) is a poetic name for death personified as a ruler who receives the dead into his realm. In texts from Ugarit, the Canaanite city on the Syrian coast, Death appears as a god called Mot, who swallows his victims, and some interpreters hear that background here. The firstborn of death (verse 13) is probably a name for a deadly disease, pictured as death's eldest son and heir, doing his father's work.

The burning sulfur in verse 15 recalls the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24), the Bible's classic picture of sudden judgment from heaven. Those in the west and the east (verse 20) may mean people living to the west and east, or those who come later and those who came before; either way, the whole world is horrified at the wicked man's end.
cultural:
Bildad's images were taken from ordinary life. The lamp in the tent (verses 5-6) was a small clay oil lamp that burned through the night in many homes; a lamp going out was a picture of a household dying, because a living family kept its lamp lit. The six different words for traps in verses 8-10 (net, mesh, trap, snare, noose, trap) come from hunting and fowling, where nets, spring traps, and hidden nooses were set along paths animals used.

The loss of name and offspring in verses 17-19 touched the deepest fear of the ancient world. A man lived on through his children, who carried his name, kept his memory, and inherited his land. To die without descendants and without anyone to remember one's name was a kind of second death. Bildad knows that all of Job's children are dead (chapter 1), and his words cannot be heard as anything but aimed at Job.
literary: After a short rebuke of Job in verses 2-4, Bildad's speech is a single sustained portrait of the wicked man's end, verses 5-21, built from clusters of images. Light and darkness frame it: the lamp goes out (verses 5-6), and the wicked man is driven from light into darkness (verse 18). Between them come the traps (verses 7-10), the terrors and disease (verses 11-14), fire in the tent (verse 15), the dry roots and withered branches (verse 16), and the lost name and offspring (verses 17-19). The final verse sums it up: “Surely such is the dwelling of the wicked and the place of one who does not know God.” Almost every image corresponds to something that has happened to Job: fire from heaven (1:16), children dead (1:19), skin diseased (2:7), honor lost. Bildad never names Job, but the portrait is drawn in his likeness.

outline.t: Bildad rebukes Job for scorning the friends
The lamp goes out, and traps close in
Terrors, disease, and the king of terrors
No tent, no root, no name, no offspring

doctrines.note: Bildad's portrait describes real consequences of wickedness that Scripture elsewhere affirms. His error is to read the portrait backward, taking suffering as proof that someone is wicked.
Verses 7-10 describe the wicked man's own schemes and feet leading him into traps. This is a true biblical insight: sin tends to entangle the one who commits it (Proverbs 5:22).

The speech ends by defining the wicked as one who does not know God. Knowing God is the Bible's deepest description of true life, but the book will show that Bildad himself does not know God as well as he thinks.

words.note: Ner, lamp, the small oil lamp that burned in a home. A lamp that keeps burning is a biblical picture of a lasting household or dynasty (1 Kings 11:36), and a lamp that goes out is a picture of its end. Bildad uses it in verse 6 for the wicked man's household.

Bekhor, firstborn, the eldest son who inherited a double share and carried the family's strength. The firstborn of death (verse 13) is a striking phrase for a fatal disease, death's strongest child. It is unclear whether a specific illness is meant.
Melekh, king. The king of terrors (verse 14) personifies death as a ruler to whom the wicked are marched as captives. The phrase gathers up the terrors that chase the wicked man in verse 11.

Shem, name. In the ancient world a name meant reputation, identity, and continuing presence through descendants. Having no name in the land (verse 17) meant being erased from memory, the fate Bildad pronounces on the wicked.

christ: Bildad's speech sets out the powers that the New Testament says Christ has confronted. The king of terrors, death personified, is the enemy Hebrews says Jesus shared our flesh and blood to defeat, in order to free those who all their lives were held in slavery by the fear of death (Hebrews 2:14-15). Paul calls death the last enemy to be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26). Where Bildad says the wicked man's lamp goes out and he is driven into darkness, Jesus calls himself the light of the world and says that whoever follows him will never walk in darkness (John 8:12). The fear of dying without a name also finds an answer in the promise that those who belong to Christ have their names written in heaven (Luke 10:20). These are thematic links, not predictions in Bildad's speech, and Bildad himself would not have meant them.

hard.q: Why does Scripture include such a cruel speech to a suffering man?
hard.a: Bildad's portrait of the wicked is aimed at a man who has lost his children to disaster and his health to disease, and it describes those very losses as the marks of one who does not know God. Readers rightly find it cruel. The book includes it because the book of Job is an argument, and it needs the friends' case in its fullest and strongest form in order to test it. Bildad is a sincere believer defending what he sees as God's justice, and much of what he says about the wicked is true in general. The problem is that he treats it as a formula that explains every case, and so he condemns an innocent man. At the end of the book God says that the friends have not spoken of him what is right (42:7). Reading Bildad's speech carefully helps readers recognize the same pattern when it appears in their own thinking and speech.

questions: Bildad never names Job, but every image fits Job's losses. What does that suggest about how words can wound even when they seem general?
The fear of being forgotten runs through verses 17-19. How does that fear show up in people today, and what does the gospel say to it?
Bildad describes the wicked as those who do not know God. What does it actually mean to know God, and how might Bildad have missed it?
